name: Dordrecht
title: Ship Thickness Measurement Dordrecht | Coasters & Dredgers
description: Thickness measurement in Dordrecht for river-sea coasters, short-sea ships and dredgers: hull, hold, tank and piping gauging at the seaport and yards.
h1: Ultrasonic Gauging for Coasters, River-Sea Ships and Dredgers in Dordrecht
intro: Dordrecht stands where the Merwede, the Noord, the Oude Maas and the Dordtsche Kil meet, a river junction crowded with barge and coastal traffic and the centre of the Drechtsteden shipbuilding region. Its seaport takes coasters and short-sea ships, river-sea vessels pass on their way to Germany, and the yards around the town build and repair dredgers, workboats and inland ships. Gauging here follows that mix. The inspection team travels from India to each vessel rather than working from any base in the area.

highlights.h: River-sea ships with low air draught
highlights.p: Coasters built to sail from the North Sea up the Rhine have low superstructures, shallow draught and box-shaped holds. Their bottom plating takes wear from shallow river berths and their hatch covers work hard, so both deserve close attention whenever these ships are gauged.

The Drechtsteden are home to dredging contractors and the yards that build for them, and hopper and cutter suction dredgers return here for maintenance. Abrasive wear in hoppers, pipe bends and discharge lines is measured on a denser grid than corrosion alone would need.

highlights.h: A seaport in the Rotterdam port area
highlights.p: Dordrecht's seaport is managed as part of the Rotterdam port area, yet its quays deal in smaller ships: coasters and short-sea traders with dry bulk and general cargo. Calls are short but regular, and a lay day gives time for holds, hatch coamings and ballast tanks.

port.h: Dordrecht: river junction, seaport and shipbuilding town
p: Dordrecht occupies an island bounded by rivers. It is the oldest town in Holland and for centuries a trading port at the meeting of the Merwede with the waters flowing towards Rotterdam and the Hollands Diep. The Beneden-Merwede leads east towards the Waal and the Rhine, the Noord runs north towards Rotterdam, and the Oude Maas and Dordtsche Kil carry seagoing ships to and from the Botlek and Moerdijk. This makes the town a crossroads for barge traffic between the North Sea ports and Germany, and for river-sea coasters that sail directly from Scandinavia, the Baltic or the British Isles to inland ports on the Rhine. The water around Dordrecht is tidal but the range is modest, and river discharge and wind move the level as much as the tide does.

The seaport on the Oude Maas and Dordtsche Kil side of the town takes seagoing coasters and short-sea ships handling dry bulk and general cargo, and it is managed within the Rotterdam port area. Ships calling here are small enough to make the river passage from the Maas comfortably, so the fleet is coastal in scale. Upriver, the Drechtsteden towns of Zwijndrecht, Papendrecht, Sliedrecht, Hendrik-Ido-Ambacht, Alblasserdam and Hardinxveld-Giessendam carry on a shipbuilding tradition that has produced generations of dredgers, tugs, inland ships and specialised workboats. Dredging contractors have their roots in the area, and their fleets come back to its yards for maintenance and conversion. River-sea vessels pass Dordrecht on almost every voyage up the Merwede, and some load or discharge at its quays.

Berth stays at the seaport are usually a day or two for cargo, and a lay day between fixtures is common for tramp coasters. At the yards a vessel may stay for weeks during a refit or conversion, and that is the setting for a full thickness programme. River conditions shape the year: high discharge in winter and spring raises levels and speeds the current, while a dry late summer can lower the Rhine enough to restrict how much a river-sea coaster can load for upriver ports. A coaster waiting for its next cargo or for river levels to recover may lie idle for days, and an idle ship with empty holds is the easiest ship to gauge. Ice on the rivers is unusual, but in a hard winter it can interrupt barge and coaster traffic for a while.

facilities.h: Seaport quays, Drechtsteden yards and lay berths
p: Gauging in and around Dordrecht takes place in three kinds of setting. At the seaport quays the work fits around a cargo operation, so holds are measured once discharged and ballast tanks once the crew has emptied and ventilated them. At the repair and conversion yards in Dordrecht and the neighbouring Drechtsteden towns, vessels are out of service with the yard's lifting gear, staging and services available, which allows a full programme to the TM plan with the class surveyor attending where a survey is due. And at lay berths along the rivers, idle coasters and workboats can be measured over several days at an unhurried pace.

The yards in this region are mostly built around inland vessels, dredgers, workboats and coastal ships rather than large deep-sea tonnage, and a manager chooses one according to the size of the vessel and the work needed. Larger short-sea ships needing a drydock usually go downriver to the Rotterdam area, Schiedam included. Inland tankers and dry-cargo barges also come out of the water in the Drechtsteden, and hull thickness readings are commonly part of their periodic certificate inspections. The same technicians and gauges serve both kinds of vessel, with the report laid out for whichever inspecting body will review it.
list: Dordrecht seaport quays — hold, hatch coaming and tank-top gauging on coasters and short-sea ships between discharge and loading.
Repair and conversion yards in the Drechtsteden — full thickness programmes on dredgers, workboats and coastal ships taken out of service.
Lay berths on the Oude Maas and Merwede — owner's condition and pre-purchase gauging on idle river-sea coasters.
Dredger maintenance periods — wear gauging on hoppers, bottom doors, suction pipes and discharge lines alongside the hull readings.
Inland vessel docking and slipway periods — bottom and side plating readings for certificate renewals.
Docks downriver at Schiedam and Rotterdam — where larger short-sea ships go, with Dordrecht readings feeding the steel plan.

context.h: Rules on the rivers: port state control, river-sea trading and EU measures
p: Seagoing ships at Dordrecht's quays are inspected under the Paris MoU, as in any Dutch port, and the coasters and river-sea ships that call are often older vessels flagged in the Netherlands, elsewhere in the EU or in the open registers. River-sea ships occupy a regulatory middle ground: on their seagoing legs they follow SOLAS and their class rules, while on the Rhine they sail under that river's navigation regulations as well. Their owners need hull condition data that satisfies the surveyor at one end of the voyage and stands up to an inspector at the other, and a single well-documented gauging serves both.

The EU's climate and recycling rules reach this fleet just as they reach ships at the coast: an Inventory of Hazardous Materials for ships calling at EU ports above the threshold tonnage, and emissions accounting under the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime for the larger ships. For a small coaster fleet, though, the pressure comes as much from age and charterer expectations as from regulation. Dredging contractors set their own standards for fleet upkeep and plan structural work between campaigns, which is why Dordrecht's dredger work concentrates in the windows when vessels are back from a project and need to be ready for the next.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging work around Dordrecht
jobs.p: The work in Dordrecht divides between short jobs on trading coasters and longer programmes on vessels in a yard. On a coaster the superintendent usually wants a focused answer, such as the state of the holds and hatch covers or a ballast tank that has started to give trouble, and the scope is set by the berth time. In a yard the programme follows the TM plan and the yard's work schedule, and the gauging team marks plates for renewal as it goes so the steel crew can start without delay. Dredgers add wear measurements to the corrosion picture. Typical scopes:
list: A river-sea coaster between cargoes at the seaport: hold sides, tank top, hatch coamings and hatch covers gauged, with bottom plating checked from the double-bottom tanks.
A trailing suction hopper dredger in a Drechtsteden yard: hopper plating, bottom-door frames and suction pipe sections measured ahead of a renewal survey.
A cutter suction dredger between projects: discharge line and floating pipeline wall thickness, with readings on the spud wells and ladder structure.
A short-sea general cargo ship before sale: pre-purchase gauging of holds, ballast tanks and deck at a lay berth while the ship is idle.
An offshore workboat during a refit: deck, crane pedestal and tank gauging, with magnetic particle testing on the pedestal welds.

logistics: Dordrecht has a main-line rail station on the route between Rotterdam and Antwerp, so a team landing at Amsterdam Schiphol or Rotterdam The Hague Airport can reach the town by train or road. Yards and seaport terminals control their gates, and the ship's agent or the yard registers the technicians before arrival. Technicians from India travel on Schengen visas, so the docking date or the expected call should reach us early; for yard work we coordinate the start with the yard's schedule rather than with the ship's arrival alone.

faqs.q: Do you gauge river-sea coasters on their Rhine voyages?
faqs.a: We gauge them where they stop, which for many is Dordrecht or another port on the route. A coaster with empty holds at a Dordrecht quay can have its holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks measured within a day if the tanks are prepared. Because these ships often use shallow river berths, we pay particular attention to bottom plating and double-bottom structure, where contact with the riverbed may have thinned or dented it.

faqs.q: Can dredger wear be measured as well as corrosion?
faqs.a: Yes. An ultrasonic reading does not care whether steel was lost to corrosion or to abrasion, so the same method serves both. On dredgers we measure the hopper, bottom doors, suction and discharge pipes and their bends on a closer grid, because wear concentrates at changes of direction. The report shows the pattern, so the owner can see where renewal is due and where it can wait for the next campaign.

faqs.q: Is hull gauging for inland vessels something you do?
faqs.a: Yes, alongside our work on seagoing ships. Inland tankers and dry-cargo barges taken out of the water at a Drechtsteden yard can be gauged on the bottom and side plating and in the tanks, with the report laid out for the inspecting body that will review it. Tell us the vessel's certificate status and the inspecting body when you enquire, and we will set the scope accordingly.

faqs.q: Where do larger ships from Dordrecht go for docking?
faqs.a: Short-sea ships too big for the Drechtsteden yards usually dock downriver in the Rotterdam area, where the yards at Schiedam and in the Botlek take larger vessels. Readings taken at Dordrecht before the docking go into the yard specification, so the yard plans its steel work on measured figures and the docking days are set accordingly.

faqs.q: Can a coaster's hatch covers be gauged during a cargo stop?
faqs.a: Usually, once the covers are stowed and safe to approach, or closed and clear of cargo gear. Top plating, skirt plates and packing channels are measured, and coaming tops and brackets are added because cracking and wastage there affect weathertightness. On coasters with folding or stacking covers, the hinges and cleats are worth a visual and dye penetrant check at the same time.
